screens.title: Ansible: The Agentless Automation Engine
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible stands out as an agentless automation engine, meaning it doesn't require any special software or agents to be installed on the network devices you manage. This is a significant advantage, as it simplifies deployment and reduces overhead in existing network infrastructures. Instead, Ansible communicates with devices primarily over standard protocols like SSH for CLI-based interactions, or NETCONF and RESTCONF for A P I-driven configurations. It uses human-readable YAML playbooks to define the desired state of your network, making automation tasks intuitive and easy to understand. For example, if you want to ensure a specific VLAN exists on a switch, you simply describe that desired state in a playbook, and Ansible handles the underlying commands or A P I calls. This abstraction allows network engineers to focus on 'what' they want to achieve rather than 'how' to achieve it, streamlining complex orchestration tasks. A common misconception is that agentless means less secure, but Ansible leverages existing secure channels like SSH, making it a robust and trusted solution. Ansible: The Agentless Automation Engine

Define desired states for your network devices.

What is Agentless Automation?

It allows engineers to quickly automate tasks without the complexities of agent installation, maintenance, or compatibility issues across various vendor platforms. screens.title: Understanding Ansible's Core Components
screens.narratorSegment: At its core, Ansible operates on a few key principles that form its architectural foundation. First, we have the Inventory file, which is essentially a list of all the devices you want to manage. Think of it as a phone book for your network, where you define hostnames, IP addresses, and group devices for easier management. Next are Playbooks, which are human-readable YAML files that describe the automation tasks to be performed. These playbooks define the desired state of your network and orchestrate complex workflows. They are the 'what to do' part of Ansible. Finally, Modules are small programs that Ansible executes on the managed hosts to perform specific tasks. For Cisco devices, Ansible provides a rich set of modules under collections like cisco. ios or cisco. nxos. These modules abstract away the complexities of CLI commands or A P I calls, allowing you to focus on the desired configuration state. For instance, the cisco. ios. ios underscore config module handles all the intricacies of configuring an IOS-XE device, so you don't have to write custom scripts for every command. Understanding how these three components interact is crucial for building effective automation solutions.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Ansible's Core Components
Architecture

Understanding Ansible's Core Components

Inventory, Playbooks, and Modules drive automation.

The Automation Flow

  • Inventory: Defines target devices.
  • Playbooks: Orchestrate tasks in YAML.
  • Modules: Execute specific actions on devices.
  • Collections: Group vendor-specific modules (e.g., `cisco.ios`).

Why This Structure Works

This modular design allows for clear separation of concerns: the inventory defines 'who' to manage, playbooks define 'what' to do, and modules define 'how' to do it. This makes Ansible highly flexible, scalable, and easy to maintain, as changes to one component don't necessarily impact others.

Ansible Core Components Diagram

Ansible Control Node
Inventory
Playbooks

Managed Devices
Key Takeaway

Ansible's architecture relies on a clear separation of inventory, playbooks, and modules to define, orchestrate, and execute automation tasks on managed devices.

screens.title: Defining Managed Hosts with Inventory
screens.narratorSegment: The Ansible inventory file is your central directory for all managed hosts. It's where you define the devices Ansible will interact with, their IP addresses or hostnames, and how they are grouped. This file can be in INI or YAML format, and it's crucial for organizing your network infrastructure. For example, you might group all your Cisco IOS-XE routers under an ios underscore routers group, allowing you to target specific automation tasks to only those devices. The inventory also allows you to define variables that apply to all hosts, or specific groups, such as ansible underscore network underscore os to specify the operating system, or connection credentials like ansible underscore user and ansible underscore password. This separation of host information from your automation logic makes your playbooks highly reusable. A common mistake is to hardcode credentials directly into playbooks; always use inventory variables or, even better, Ansible Vault for sensitive data. By structuring your inventory effectively, you lay the groundwork for scalable and maintainable network automation. content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Defining Managed Hosts with Inventory
Practical Scenario

Defining Managed Hosts with Inventory

Grouping devices for targeted automation.

Key Aspects of Inventory

  • Lists hostnames or IP addresses of managed devices.
  • Organizes devices into logical groups (e.g., `[ios_routers]`).
  • Defines connection variables (e.g., `ansible_user`, `ansible_password`).
  • Can include global variables for all hosts (`[all:vars]`).

Best Practice: Variable Separation

Storing connection details and other host-specific variables in the inventory file, rather than hardcoding them in playbooks, enhances reusability and security. For sensitive data like passwords, always use Ansible Vault for encryption.

inventory.ini Example
[ios_routers] # Define a group for IOS-XE routers
router1.example.com
router2.example.com

[all:vars] # Variables applicable to all hosts
ansible_network_os=ios
ansible_user=admin
ansible_password=cisco # Use Ansible Vault for production
ansible_become=yes
ansible_become_method=enable
ansible_become_pass=cisco # Use Ansible Vault for production
Common Mistake

Hardcoding sensitive credentials directly into playbooks or unencrypted inventory files. Always use Ansible Vault for passwords and API keys.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Crafting Your First Playbook
Playbook Development

Crafting Your First Playbook

Automating NTP configuration with YAML.

Playbook Structure Essentials

  • Starts with `---` (YAML document separator).
  • `name`: Descriptive title for the playbook.
  • `hosts`: Specifies target host group from inventory.
  • `gather_facts: no`: Prevents fact gathering for network devices.
  • `connection: network_cli`: Defines connection type.
  • `tasks`: A list of actions to perform.

Module in Focus: `cisco.ios.ios_config`

This module is designed for configuring Cisco IOS-XE devices. It allows you to specify configuration `lines` within a `parents` block, ensuring precise and idempotent configuration management. The `match` and `replace` parameters control how existing configurations are handled.

ntp_config.yml Example
---
- name: Configure NTP on Cisco IOS-XE devices
  hosts: ios_routers
  gather_facts: no
  connection: network_cli

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure NTP server is configured
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines:
          - ntp server 10.0.0.1 prefer
          - ntp server 10.0.0.2
        parents: "ntp"
        match: exact
        replace: line
      register: ntp_result

    - name: Display NTP configuration changes
      debug:
        var: ntp_result
Key Takeaway

Ansible playbooks, written in YAML, define the desired state of your network through tasks that leverage specific modules like `cisco.ios.ios_config` for precise configuration management.

screens.title: Idempotency: The Power of Predictable Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency is a fundamental concept in Ansible and a cornerstone of reliable automation. It means that executing the same playbook multiple times will consistently produce the same network state as executing it just once, without causing any unintended side effects or errors if the configuration already exists. This is incredibly valuable in network automation, as it allows you to run playbooks repeatedly without worrying about breaking existing configurations or introducing inconsistencies. For instance, if you run a playbook to ensure an NTP server is configured, and that server is already present, Ansible will detect this and report no changes, rather than attempting to re-add it or causing an error. The cisco. ios. ios underscore config module, for example, achieves idempotency through parameters like match and replace. Using match. exact and replace. line ensures that only the specified configuration lines are managed within a parent block, preventing accidental overwrites of other, unrelated configurations. A common mistake is to use match. none or replace. config without fully understanding their implications, which could lead to unintended configuration deletions. Always prioritize testing in a lab environment to confirm idempotent behavior.

Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Idempotency: Predictable Automation
Core Principle

Idempotency: The Power of Predictable Automation

Running playbooks multiple times yields the same result.

What Idempotency Means

  • Operation produces same result regardless of how many times it's run.
  • Prevents unintended side effects or errors on existing configurations.
  • Crucial for reliable and repeatable network automation.
  • Ansible modules are designed to be idempotent by default.

Idempotency in `cisco.ios.ios_config`

Parameters like `match: exact` and `replace: line` are key. `match: exact` ensures only specified lines are considered, while `replace: line` ensures only those lines are added or updated, leaving other configurations untouched. This prevents accidental overwrites or deletions within a configuration block.

Idempotency in Action

Ansible Playbook
Run 1: Config Applied
Run 2: No Changes
Ensuring consistent network state every time.
Common Mistake

Misusing `replace: config` or `match: none` can lead to unintended configuration overwrites or deletions. Always understand their implications and test thoroughly.

screens.title: Executing and Verifying Ansible Playbooks
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've crafted your Ansible playbook, the next step is to execute it. You'll use the ansible-playbook command, specifying your inventory file and the playbook itself. For example, ansible-playbook -i inventory. ini ntp underscore config. yml will connect to each device in the ios underscore routers group, apply the NTP configuration, and report any changes. A critical best practice before applying any changes to a production network is to use the --check flag. This performs a 'dry run' of the playbook, showing you exactly what changes Ansible *would* make without actually applying them. This is invaluable for previewing configurations and catching potential issues before they impact your live network. Always test your playbooks thoroughly in a lab environment first, and use --check as a final verification step. After execution, you can verify the changes directly on the network device using standard CLI commands, such as show running-config pipe section ntp for our NTP example. This ensures that the desired state defined in your playbook has been successfully applied and is operational. Remember, verification is just as important as execution in any automation workflow.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Executing and Verifying Playbooks
Workflow

Executing and Verifying Ansible Playbooks

Safely apply configurations and preview changes.

Key Execution Commands

  • `ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini playbook.yml`: Executes the playbook.
  • `ansible-playbook --check`: Performs a dry run, showing changes without applying.
  • `ansible-playbook --diff`: Shows the differences that would be applied.
  • Always specify the inventory file with `-i`.

Verification Best Practices

After running a playbook, always verify the changes directly on the network device using appropriate `show` commands. This confirms that the automation achieved the desired state and helps catch any unexpected behavior. Testing in a lab environment before production deployment is non-negotiable.

ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini ntp_config.yml --check

# changed: [router2.example.com]
# 
# PLAY RECAP *******************************************************************
# router1.example.com : ok=1    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
# router2.example.com : ok=1    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0

# ntp server 10.0.0.2

Always use `ansible-playbook --check` to preview changes and thoroughly test playbooks in a lab environment before deploying to production.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Scalable Automation with Variables
Best Practices

Scalable Automation with Ansible Variables

Separate data from logic for reusable playbooks.

Where to Define Variables

  • Inventory File: For host-specific or group-specific variables.
  • `group_vars/`: Directory for variables applying to entire groups.
  • `host_vars/`: Directory for variables unique to individual hosts.
  • Playbook: Directly within the playbook (less common for reusability).

Benefits of Variable Usage

Variables make playbooks generic and adaptable. A single playbook can configure many devices with different parameters, reducing code duplication and improving maintainability. This is essential for managing large and complex network infrastructures efficiently.

Example: Host-Specific Variables
# host_vars/router1.example.com.yml
loopback_ip: 192.168.1.1/32

# host_vars/router2.example.com.yml
loopback_ip: 192.168.1.2/32

# In your playbook (e.g., configure_loopback.yml)
---
- name: Configure Loopback Interface
  hosts: ios_routers
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Loopback0 is configured
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines:
          - ip address {{ loopback_ip }}
        parents: "interface Loopback0"
Pro-Tip

Use `ansible-inventory --list` to inspect your inventory and verify that variables are being loaded correctly for your hosts and groups.

screens.title: Protecting Sensitive Data with Ansible Vault
screens.narratorSegment: Security is paramount in any automation solution, especially when dealing with network devices that require credentials. Storing sensitive information like ansible underscore password or A P I keys in plain text within your inventory or playbooks is a significant security risk and should be strictly avoided in any production environment. This is where Ansible Vault comes in. Ansible Vault is a powerful feature that allows you to encrypt sensitive data, such as passwords, A P I keys, or other confidential information, within your playbooks or variable files. When you encrypt a file with Ansible Vault, it becomes unreadable without the correct password. Ansible will prompt you for the vault password when it needs to access encrypted data during playbook execution. This ensures that your sensitive data remains protected, even if your automation repository is compromised. Always prioritize security by encrypting sensitive data and adhering to the principle of least privilege for automation user accounts. This means granting only the necessary permissions for automation tasks, minimizing potential attack surfaces. Implementing Ansible Vault is a non-negotiable best practice for secure network automation.

Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Protecting Sensitive Data with Ansible Vault
Security

Protecting Sensitive Data with Ansible Vault

Encrypting passwords and API keys.

Why Ansible Vault is Essential

  • Encrypts sensitive data (passwords, API keys, etc.).
  • Protects data at rest within your automation repository.
  • Requires a vault password for decryption during execution.
  • Prevents security risks associated with plain text credentials.

Security Best Practices

Always encrypt sensitive data using Ansible Vault. Implement the principle of least privilege for automation user accounts, ensuring they only have the necessary permissions to perform their tasks. Regularly review and rotate credentials.

Ansible Vault Workflow
# Create an encrypted file
ansible-vault create host_vars/router1.example.com.yml

# Edit an encrypted file
ansible-vault edit group_vars/all.yml

# Encrypt an existing file
ansible-vault encrypt my_secret_file.txt

# Decrypt a file
ansible-vault decrypt my_secret_file.txt

# View an encrypted file
ansible-vault view my_secret_file.txt

# Run playbook with vault password
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini playbook.yml --ask-vault-pass
Security Warning

Never store unencrypted passwords or API keys in version control systems. A breach could expose critical network access credentials.

Module 6›Chapter 6.1›Practical: Configure VLANs
Hands-on Activity

Practical: Configure VLANs with Ansible

Apply your knowledge to a real-world scenario.

Scenario: VLAN Configuration

You need to create two new VLANs (VLAN 10 for "Users" and VLAN 20 for "Servers") on a Cisco IOS-XE router using Ansible.

Instructions

  1. Create an `inventory.ini` file for your Cisco IOS-XE device.
  2. Create a playbook named `configure_vlans.yml`.
  3. Use `cisco.ios.ios_config` to add VLAN 10 and VLAN 20.
  4. Run the playbook and verify VLANs on your device.
Key Takeaway

Hands-on practice with Ansible playbooks and modules is essential for building practical network automation skills.

Starter Code
# inventory.ini
[ios_routers]
your_router_ip_or_hostname

[all:vars]
ansible_network_os=ios
ansible_user=your_ssh_username
ansible_password=your_ssh_password
ansible_become=yes
ansible_become_method=enable
ansible_become_pass=your_enable_password

# configure_vlans.yml
---
- name: Configure VLANs on Cisco IOS-XE
  hosts: ios_routers
  gather_facts: no

  tasks:
    - name: Create VLAN 10 and VLAN 20
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines:
          - name Users
        parents: "vlan 10"
      # TODO: Add configuration for VLAN 20 here following the same pattern
      # ...
      register: vlan_result

    - name: Display VLAN configuration changes
      debug:
        var: vlan_result.updates

Next are Playbooks, which are human-readable YAML files that describe the automation tasks to be performed. These playbooks define the desired state of your network and orchestrate complex workflows. They are the 'what to do' part of Ansible. Finally, Modules are small programs that Ansible executes on the managed hosts to perform specific tasks. For Cisco devices, Ansible provides a rich set of modules under collections like cisco. ios or cisco. nxos. These modules abstract away the complexities of CLI commands or A P I calls, allowing you to focus on the desired configuration state. The Ansible inventory file is your central directory for all managed hosts. It's where you define the devices Ansible will interact with, their IP addresses or hostnames, and how they are grouped. This file can be in INI or YAML format, and it's crucial for organizing your network infrastructure. For example, you might group all your Cisco IOS-XE routers under an ios underscore routers group, allowing you to target specific automation tasks to only those devices. The inventory also allows you to define variables that apply to all hosts, or specific groups, such as ansible underscore network underscore os to specify the operating system, or connection credentials like ansible underscore user and ansible underscore password. Idempotency is a fundamental concept in Ansible and a cornerstone of reliable automation. It means that executing the same playbook multiple times will consistently produce the same network state as executing it just once, without causing any unintended side effects or errors if the configuration already exists. Let's recap some of the core concepts we've covered in this chapter. First, Ansible itself is an open-source automation engine that simplifies software provisioning, configuration management, and application deployment. Its agentless nature, using SSH or APIs, makes it incredibly easy to integrate into existing network infrastructures. Next, the Inventory is a crucial file, typically in INI or YAML format, that defines all the managed hosts and groups of hosts that Ansible will operate on. It's your network's address book, organizing devices for targeted automation. Finally, Playbooks are YAML files that define a set of tasks to be executed on these managed hosts. They orchestrate your automation workflows, describing the desired state of your network in a human-readable format. Understanding these three fundamental components is essential for anyone looking to leverage Ansible for network automation.

Continuing our review of key concepts, let's look at some advanced principles that ensure robust and secure automation. First, Modules are discrete units of code that Ansible executes on managed hosts to perform specific tasks. These are the 'how-to' instructions, abstracting complex CLI or A P I calls into simple, reusable actions, like cisco. ios. ios underscore config. Next, Idempotency is a critical property of an operation that ensures executing it multiple times produces the same result as executing it once, without causing unintended side effects. This guarantees predictable and reliable network configurations. Finally, Ansible Vault is a vital security feature used to encrypt sensitive data, such as passwords or A P I keys, within playbooks or variable files. It protects your confidential information, preventing security risks in production environments. Mastering these advanced concepts is crucial for building efficient, reliable, and secure network automation solutions.
